claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its FCC quaternary and ternary subsets arise from differences in local lattice distortion.
Mechanical-property differences among these alloys arise from differences in their stacking-fault-energy distributions.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has a broader distribution of local lattice distortions than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
A broader distribution of local lattice distortions enhances dislocation interactions.
Enhanced dislocation interactions promote sustained strain hardening.
Reducing the number of constituents from five to four or three narrows the distribution of local lattice distortions.
A narrower distortion distribution leads to earlier strain localization.
Earlier strain localization produces lower ductility.
The compared alloys can be prepared as single-phase FCC microstructures using identical thermomechanical treatments.
Atomic-size mismatches in the quinary alloy create a wider distribution of local lattice distortions.
Variation in electronic structure in the quinary alloy contributes to a wider distribution of local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortion modifies the stacking-fault-energy landscape.
The stacking-fault-energy landscape affects dislocation mobility and interactions.
Fewer-component alloys have a more uniform stacking-fault-energy distribution because they have less lattice distortion.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary alloys will exhibit lower uniform elongation.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the ternary alloys will exhibit lower uniform elongation, with a larger reduction than the quaternary alloys.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit less sustained strain hardening than the quinary baseline.
The predicted relationships apply to confirmed single-phase FCC specimens tested in monotonic tension at room temperature and constant strain rate after identical thermomechanical processing.
